They are rallying around Meloni’s decision to flex diplomatic muscle. However, the business establishment is getting nervous. **La Stampa** and **Il Sole 24 Ore** are warning that escalating a judicial disagreement into a full-blown diplomatic rift with a key economic partner like Switzerland is a high-risk gamble. They highlight the response from Swiss President Guy Parmelin, who lectured Rome on the separation of powers. The takeaway is that Meloni is caught between the need to show strength to her domestic base and the reality that she cannot force a Swiss prosecutor to change the law. Moving from the mountains to the grinding gears of the government coalition, the internal friction is heating up. The issue is identity, and the catalyst is Tommy Robinson. **La Repubblica** and **Il Fatto Quotidiano** are feasting on the discord caused by Matteo Salvini hosting the British far-right extremist at the Ministry of Transport. But the real news isn't the guest; it's the reaction from within the majority. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, usually the diplomat, drew a hard line in **Corriere della Sera**, stating that Robinson is "incompatible with our values." This has emboldened the centrist opposition, with Carlo Calenda praising Tajani’s stance. Salvini is fighting a war on two fronts. While fending off Tajani in the center, he is trying to secure his right flank against General Roberto Vannacci, the controversial MEP elected on the League’s ticket who is rumored to be starting his own party. **Il Giornale** reports Salvini’s warning shot delivered from a stage in Abruzzo: "Whoever leaves the League ends up in nothing." It is a clear message to the General: you are famous because of my symbol, do not mistake your popularity for political autonomy. The synthesis here is a government struggling to define where the "Right" ends and the "Far Right" begins, a distinction that is becoming increasingly expensive for Italy's international reputation. Turning to the geopolitical stage, the "friendship" with the incoming Trump administration is hitting its first significant speed bump, and it involves military honor. **Libero** and **Il Giornale**—usually the first to cheer for Trump—are visibly stung by the President-elect's comments that NATO allies "stayed in the rear" during the Afghanistan conflict. For Italy, which lost 53 soldiers and had over 700 wounded, this is an open wound. Prime Minister Meloni issued a formal rebuke, stating that "friendship needs respect." **La Verità** frames this as a necessary correction, noting that Italy commanded the Western sector and was engaged in heavy combat, not rear-guard duties. **La Repubblica** analyzes this with a touch of cynicism, suggesting that Meloni is discovering the hard limits of her Atlanticist alignment. The takeaway is harsh but clear: Trump’s "America First" does not have a "Best Friends" exemption clause, and Rome is realizing that historical loyalty might not buy the leverage they hoped for in the new Washington. But before we go, a moment of history in the making within the Vatican walls. **AGI** reports that after nearly nine months of darkness following the transition, the mosaic medallion of the new Pontiff has finally been illuminated in the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls. The portrait of Pope Leo XIV, elected last May, now shines alongside his 266 predecessors. It is a centuries-old tradition: only the reigning Pope’s face is lit, while the others fade into the shadows of the nave. A bright circle of gold in the Roman gloom, signaling that the machine of the Church, much like the country surrounding it, keeps turning regardless of the noise outside. That is the state of the country today. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-01-26
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-01-26/2026-01-26-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Monday 26 and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. Let’s get straight to the pulse of the nation. The institutional war between the Government and the Judiciary has reached a boiling point after a controversial social media post by the Magistrates' Union secretary; in the Middle East, a diplomatic incident involving Italian Carabinieri and an armed Israeli settler has triggered a summons to the Farnesina; meanwhile, the earth is literally opening up in Sicily, with half the town of Niscemi sliding down a hill, displacing over a thousand people. In the north, the Olympic torch is already burning—but with controversy, as Minister Abodi preemptively silences the singer Ghali regarding Gaza; and finally, a tragic update to the Anguillara femicide, where the parents of the killer have taken their own lives, crushed by public shame. But we begin with the open warfare consuming the Ministry of Justice, a clash that has moved from parliamentary debate to what **Libero** and **Il Giornale** are characterizing as a grotesque institutional suicide by the magistracy. The spark was a now-deleted post by Rocco Maruotti, the secretary of the ANM—the National Association of Magistrates. Maruotti posted an image of Alex Jeffrey Pretti, a man killed by federal agents in Minneapolis, and juxtaposed it with the Nordio Justice Reform, captioning it: "Also this state murder will remain unpunished in that 'democracy' whose judicial system inspires the Meloni-Nordio reform." It was a clumsy attempt to criticize the separation of careers, but the backlash was instant. Justice Minister Carlo Nordio, usually reserved, called the comparison "disgusting" and the subsequent apology "unacceptable," suggesting it reveals an intellect inadequate for the office. For the Right-wing press, this is the smoking gun they have been waiting for: proof that the judiciary is politicized, anti-American, and ideologically opposed to the government. However, if you look at the **AGI** wire services, there is a darker undercurrent to this paranoia. The Magistrates are on edge because of rumors that the Ministry has installed "remote control" software on their computers capable of turning on webcams—a claim the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) had to formally deny today. **La Repubblica** frames this as a total breakdown of trust: on one side, a government pushing a reform that separates judges from prosecutors; on the other, a judiciary that feels besieged, spied upon, and is now lashing out with communication blunders that undermine its own authority. Moving from the internal courts to the external borders, the concept of national sovereignty is being tested on two very different fronts. First, in the West Bank, where **La Stampa** and **Corriere della Sera** report a humiliation for the Italian uniform. Two Carabinieri, part of a diplomatic protection unit at the Jerusalem Consulate, were forced to their knees and held at gunpoint by an armed Israeli settler—not a soldier—while conducting a site visit. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has summoned the Israeli ambassador, demanding answers. While **Il Giornale** reports the facts, the centrist and leftist press are asking a harder question: if Italy cannot protect its own paramilitary police from civilians in an occupied territory, what is the weight of Rome's influence in Tel Aviv? Simultaneously, a mirror image of this sovereignty anxiety is playing out in Milan regarding the upcoming Olympics. **La Repubblica** and **Il Fatto Quotidiano** are amplifying concerns about the presence of U.S. ICE agents (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) operating on Italian soil to protect American dignitaries. Following the violent tactics used by ICE in Minneapolis, the Italian Left is petitioning to ban them, fearing "Trump's squads" in Cortina. The Viminale has issued a denial, stating ICE will not have operational powers, but the narrative synthesis is clear: from the West Bank to the Alps, the Meloni government is struggling to assert Italian jurisdiction against its own allies. While the politicians debate jurisdiction, the physical infrastructure of the country is failing. In Sicily, the situation in Niscemi has gone from an emergency to a catastrophe. **Il Sole 24 Ore** reports that the landslide front has widened to four kilometers. A thousand people have been evacuated, schools are closed, and the Vice President of the Regional Assembly warns, "Half the city is collapsing." This isn't just bad weather; it is the bill coming due for decades of hydrogeological neglect. The contrast with the government's grand projects is stark. As **Fanpage** and **La Stampa** point out, while Niscemi slides into the valley, Matteo Salvini is in a heated battle with the Court of Auditors over the Bridge on the Straits of Messina. The magistrates have warned that the government's new decree reduces controls and oversight on the massive project; Salvini calls their interference "incredible." The takeaway is a country split in two: one spending billions on future engineering marvels, and another unable to keep existing towns from falling off the map. Briefly updating a story we covered yesterday regarding the horror in Anguillara: the tragedy has compounded. Following the femicide of Federica Torzullo, the parents of the confessing killer, Claudio Carlomagno, were found dead by suicide. **Corriere della Sera** reports that prosecutors are opening a file for "instigation to suicide," investigating whether the "social media pillorying"—the relentless online attacks against the family—drove the elderly couple to their deaths. It is a grim reminder of the toxic speed of digital justice. But before we go, a discovery in the archives that reminds us of Italian ingenuity before the industrial age. **AGI** reports that a researcher in Padua has uncovered a document from January 26, 1604—exactly 422 years ago today. It is essentially the first patent for a pasta machine. A man named Bortolamio Veronese, nicknamed "L'Abbondanza" (The Abundance), registered a "torcio bigolaro," a wooden press to mass-produce *bigoli* pasta. It’s a small, dusty piece of history, but it signals that four centuries ago, while Europe was fighting wars of religion, someone in Veneto was already figuring out how to make dinner more efficient. That is the state of the country today. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-01-27
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-01-27/2026-01-27-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Tuesday 27 and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. Let’s get straight to the headlines. The ground is still moving in Sicily, where the Niscemi landslide has turned into a full-blown catastrophe with fifteen hundred people displaced; in Rome, the Senate marked Holocaust Remembrance Day, but not without political friction as Liliana Segre warned against using Gaza to erase the Shoah; meanwhile, a diplomatic crisis has opened with Tehran after Iran summoned the Italian ambassador over Minister Tajani’s comments on the Revolutionary Guards; in the Alps, a breakthrough in the Crans-Montana tragedy as Switzerland finally agrees to a joint investigation; and finally, a violent flashpoint in Milan, where a police shooting in the drug-dealing district of Rogoredo has reignited the debate on security and self-defense. But we begin in Milan, where the intersection of drug crime, immigration, and police rules of engagement has resulted in a death that is already polarizing the country along predictable political lines. Yesterday evening, in the notorious "boschetto" of Rogoredo—Milan’s open-air drug market—a police officer in plain clothes shot and killed a 28-year-old Moroccan national, Abderrahim Mansouri. The dynamics are the subject of intense scrutiny by the judiciary. According to **Il Giornale** and **Libero**, the officer fired in legitimate self-defense after the suspect, described as a "boss of the drug trade" with a history of resisting arrest, pointed a gun at him in the dark. That gun, however, turned out to be a replica—a fake weapon without a red cap. For the Right-wing press and Matteo Salvini, who immediately stated "I stand with the policeman without ifs or buts," this is a clear-cut case of an agent forced to make a split-second decision against a dangerous criminal. However, the narrative shifts significantly when you read **Fanpage** and **La Repubblica**. They highlight that the officer is now under investigation for voluntary homicide, a necessary technical step, but one that underscores the gravity of the act. **Fanpage** challenges the triumphalist narrative of the city administration, noting that despite Mayor Beppe Sala’s claims of cleaning up Rogoredo, the area remains a "Far West." The center-left is caught in a difficult position: trying to support state security while questioning the use of lethal force against a man holding a toy gun. The takeaway here is a renewed clash over the "Safety Decree" and the legal protections afforded to officers, with the Government pushing to shield agents from what they call "automatic indictments." Moving from the urban crisis in the North to the geological crisis in the South, the situation in Niscemi has escalated from an emergency to an existential threat for the town. As we reported yesterday, a landslide is consuming the Sicilian hillside, but today **Corriere della Sera** and **Il Sole 24 Ore** report that the fracture has widened to four kilometers. The number of evacuees has jumped to 1,500, and the head of Civil Protection, Fabio Ciciliano, was blunt: "The entire hill is collapsing." But the physical collapse has triggered a financial battle. **La Repubblica** and **La Stampa** are amplifying a specific political demand led by PD Secretary Elly Schlein, who visited the site today. Her argument is fiscal: she is demanding that the government divert the billions earmarked for the controversial Bridge over the Straits of Messina to immediately fund the hydrogeological safety of the island. It is a potent political weapon, pitting a future, theoretical mega-project against a present, tangible disaster where citizens are watching their homes slide into the valley. Turning to the diplomatic front, Italy finds itself walking a tightrope between two very different international disputes. First, there is high tension with Tehran. **AGI** and **Il Messaggero** report that the Iranian Foreign Ministry summoned the Italian Ambassador, Paola Amadei, to protest violently against Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani. Tajani had proposed listing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps—the Pasdaran—as a terrorist organization. While the government holds firm, **Il Giornale** frames this as Italy finally showing a spine against the Ayatollahs, despite the economic risks. Simultaneously, there is a rare diplomatic win regarding the Swiss border. Following the tragedy in Crans-Montana, where Italian nationals died in a nightclub fire, the Swiss government has capitulated to Italian pressure. **Libero** frames this explicitly as a victory for Premier Meloni, noting that Bern has agreed to "joint investigative teams"—a request previously snubbed. The Ambassador, who had been recalled to Rome in protest, will likely return, but the message from Palazzo Chigi is clear: Italy is demanding extraterritorial oversight when its citizens are victims of negligence abroad, a muscular stance that is playing well with the government's base. But before we go, a look at the Venice Lagoon, where an invasion of a different kind is worrying scientists. **Il Giornale** reports on the spread of the *Mnemiopsis leidyi*, commonly known as the "sea walnut." It looks like a jellyfish, but it’s a ctenophore, and while it doesn't sting humans, it is a voracious predator of plankton and fish larvae. It’s an invasive species that has already devastated ecosystems in the Black Sea, and its proliferation in Venice is being called "worse than the blue crab." It is a quiet, biological reminder that while we worry about political borders, the environmental ones are changing faster than we can legislate. That is the state of the country today. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-01-29
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-01-29/2026-01-29-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Thursday, January 29th, and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. We begin with the blitz. The island of Sicily is quite literally sliding into the sea, with a landslide in Niscemi now exceeding the volume of the infamous Vajont disaster. The Constitutional Court has delivered a stinging rebuke to the government’s "zero tolerance" highway code, ruling that drug traces alone are not enough to strip a license. Tensions rise in the classroom as the Ministry of Education authorizes metal detectors in schools to combat youth violence. In foreign affairs, rumors of a Ukraine truce brokered by Donald Trump are circulating, though dismissed by Nato officials in Rome. And finally, the government has been forced to scrap a controversial "shield" for employers underpaying workers from the PNRR decree, reportedly after a quiet intervention from the President of the Republic. But the earth is moving in Sicily, and that is where we must start. The situation in Niscemi, a town in the province of Caltanissetta, has graduated from a local emergency to a national political crisis. The technical numbers provided by *Il Sole Ventiquattro Ore* are terrifying: a landslide front of four and a half kilometers, involving 350 million cubic meters of earth. For context, the head of Civil Protection, Fabio Ciciliano, stated on SkyTG24 that this mass is nearly one and a half times the size of the landslide that caused the Vajont dam disaster in 1963. While thankfully no one has died, 1,300 people are displaced, the town is cracking apart, and the finger-pointing has begun in earnest. The political fault lines are as deep as the geological ones. On the left, *La Repubblica* and the opposition parties are demanding immediate accountability, calling for the resignation of Civil Protection Minister Nello Musumeci—who was previously the Governor of Sicily—and demanding Premier Giorgia Meloni report to Parliament. Their narrative is one of criminal negligence and ignored warnings. Conversely, the government defense, led by *Libero* and *Il Giornale*, frames this as a legacy issue, a disaster thirty years in the making that the current administration has inherited, not caused. Governor Renato Schifani, attempting to dodge the blame, claimed in *Corriere della Sera* that the municipality never sent an alarm in the last nine years—a defense that sounds thin given the scale of the disaster. But the real, structural conflict here isn't just about who ignored the cracks in the ground; it represents a brutal battle over resources. As the region cries out for emergency money to rebuild roads and stabilize hillsides, the Sicilian assembly voted to divert funds earmarked for Matteo Salvini’s crown jewel project—the Bridge over the Strait of Messina—to fix the hydrogeological instability instead. Salvini, the Minister of Infrastructure, immediately fired back, stating, "The Bridge funds are not to be touched." This sets up a vicious internal conflict within the Right: the ideological necessity of building a bridge to connect the island, versus the practical reality that the island itself is crumbling before the bridge can even be built. Moving from the laws of physics to the laws of the land, the Constitutional Court has thrown a wrench into the government’s signature security agenda. In a ruling that *La Stampa* and legal experts seek to highlight as a victory for due process, the Court declared that Article 187 of the Highway Code is partially illegitimate. Until yesterday, under the strict "drug driving" rules championed by Matteo Salvini, a driver could be convicted simply for testing positive for drug traces, even if those traces were from consumption days or weeks prior. The Court has ruled that this is unconstitutional: to be punished criminally, a driver must be in an actual "state of alteration" while behind the wheel. This is a significant blow to the "law and order" narrative of the ruling coalition. While *Il Giornale* and *Libero* are downplaying the rebuke, focusing on the safety aspects, the opposition press equates this to a rejection of populist jurisprudence. It essentially forces the police to return to a more complex, evidential standard—proving impairment, not just presence—which changes the mechanics of law enforcement on Italian roads overnight. Meanwhile, deep in the bureaucratic machinery of Rome, a quieter but equally significant institutional clash took place regarding the PNRR, the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. According to *Il Fatto Quotidiano* and later confirmed by *Corriere della Sera*, the government intended to include a "shield" in the latest decree. This provision would have allowed entrepreneurs who had underpaid workers on PNRR projects to avoid paying arrears if they simply "fixed" the situation moving forward. It was a deregulation designed to speed up projects and protect businesses. However, the clause vanished before the decree reached the Cabinet. Sources indicate this was due to "moral suasion" from the Quirinale—the office of President Sergio Mattarella—which flagged the norm as unconstitutional and unjust to workers. It is a classic example of the "invisible hand" of the Italian presidency keeping the legislative machine within the guardrails, a story often missed if you only look at the shouting matches in Parliament. But before we go, let's look up toward the heavens—or at least, the roof of St. Peter's Basilica. In a move that blends the sacred with the distinctly profane, *ANSA* reports that plans are underway to expand a refreshment point on the roof of the Vatican, effectively creating a "Bistrot on the Dome." While the Basilica insists it will remain a "sober place," the idea of sipping a cappuccino or perhaps an aperitivo while looking down on Bernini’s colonnade has purists clutching their rosaries and tourists checking their wallets. It seems that even in the Eternal City, the hospitality sector is the one religion that converts everyone. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-01-30
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-01-30/2026-01-30-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Friday, January 30th, and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. We begin with the blitz. The Italian job market delivers a surprise jolt of optimism, with *Il Sole Ventiquattro Ore* reporting unemployment has fallen to 5.6%, the lowest figure since 2004, a number the government will surely parade all weekend. In Sicily, the Niscemi landslide scandal deepens; *Corriere della Sera* reveals a 2022 dossier explicitly warned of "very high risk" in the exact spot that collapsed, proving the emergency was foretold but ignored. Following up on the security measures discussed yesterday, Turin is bracing for impact as the "Askatasuna" social center refuses the Prefect's mediation, with *La Stampa* warning of three separate marches converging on the city center tomorrow. On the international front, *Il Fatto Quotidiano* reports that Donald Trump is dusting off the "Italygate" conspiracy theory, alleging Italian satellites were used to rig the 2020 US election—a headache Rome really didn't need. And finally, students take note: the Ministry has confirmed that Latin is back for the Classical lyceum and Mathematics for the Scientific track in the 2026 Maturità exams. But we must open with the heavy artillery firing inside the Palace of Justice. The inauguration of the Judicial Year is usually a ceremony of ermine robes, polite applause, and dry statistics. Today, however, it turned into an open battlefield between the executive branch and the judiciary. The spark was the government's proposed referendum on the separation of careers—splitting judges from prosecutors. The First President of the Court of Cassation, Pasquale D’Ascola, issued a grave warning from the podium, defining the current unity of the judiciary as a "cornerstone" of the constitutional system and implying that the reform threatens judicial independence. The government’s response was immediate and unusually aggressive. Justice Minister Carlo Nordio, sitting in the same room, took the microphone and declared it "blasphemous"—his exact word—to suggest that the government’s reform undermines independence. This is a semantic escalation that signals a total breakdown working relationship. *La Repubblica* and the *Mediaset* papers are treating this like two different realities. The center-left press frames D’Ascola’s speech as a desperate defense of the Constitution against a hostile takeover. *Il Giornale* and *Libero*, conversely, frame Nordio’s "blasphemy" comment as a righteous crusade against a caste of untouchables who refuse to be reformed. The stakes here are structural. This isn't just bickering; it is the prelude to a referendum that could fundamentally rewrite the balance of power in Italy. As *Il Fatto Quotidiano* notes with its usual prosecutorial zeal, if the separation of careers passes—and the polls suggest it might—the Italian judiciary will lose its monolithic power structure. The "war of the robes" isn't coming; it is already here, and it is being fought on live television in front of the Head of State. Moving from the courtroom to the Parliament, the political temperature reached a boiling point over who is allowed inside the "Temple of Democracy." Chaos erupted at Montecitorio this morning when a League deputy, Domenico Furgiuele, attempted to host a press conference featuring CasaPound, the neo-fascist movement, to present a proposal on "Remigration." The mere presence of CasaPound inside the Chamber triggered a physical and vocal revolt from the opposition. MPs from the Democratic Party, Five Star Movement, and the Green-Left Alliance physically occupied the press room, waving copies of the Constitution and singing "Bella Ciao" until the event was cancelled for "public order reasons." The narrative split here is sharp and reveals the fragility of the current political discourse. *La Stampa* and *Fanpage* describe the attempted conference as an institutional obscenity, a legitimization of the far-right within the halls of Parliament. They highlight the "Remigration" topic as a direct import of xenophobic rhetoric. On the flip side, *Libero* and *La Verità* are attacking the Left’s reaction as illiberal, arguing that blocking a press conference—even one by extremists—is an act of censorship, with *Il Giornale* asking why the Left is allowed to dictate who speaks in a public building. It is a classic Italian stalemate: the Right tests the boundaries of historical memory, the Left mobilizes the resistance, and the actual business of legislating grinds to a halt amidst shouting matches. Meanwhile, moving to the engine room of the economy, there is a changing of the guard that is far more consequential than the shouting in Parliament. While the unemployment numbers are good, the institutions managing the money are shifting. *Il Sole Ventiquattro Ore* reports that Luigi Federico Signorini is stepping down as Director General of the Bank of Italy for personal reasons. He will be replaced by Paolo Angelini. This might seem like boring bureaucratic shuffling, but in Rome, personnel is policy. Signorini was a pillar of the old guard; his exit marks another step in the slow potential reshaping of Italy's independent authorities. With the economy showing signs of life—employment is up—the struggle now is over who controls the levers of stability. But before we go, let's turn to the nightmare of every Italian high school student. The Ministry of Education has released the subjects for the 2026 "Maturità" exams, and there is no mercy this year. As reported by *Corriere della Sera*, the pendulum has swung back to tradition. Students at the *Liceo Classico* will face a version of Latin—the subject they dread most—while the *Scientifico* gets hit with Mathematics. But the real sting is in the oral exam: Minister Valditara has tweaked the rules so that the interview will cover four specific disciplines, making it much harder to "wing it." It is a clear signal that the era of the "light" exam, a hangover from the pandemic years, is officially over. The "notti prima degli esami" this June are going to be very long indeed. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-01-31
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-01-31/2026-01-31-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Saturday, January 31st, and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. We begin with the blitz. The streets of Turin turned into a combat zone this afternoon as the demonstration for the "Askatasuna" social center devolved into guerrilla warfare, with *La Stampa* reporting police charges, tear gas, and burning barricades in Corso Regina Margherita. On the economic front, the government receives an unexpected gift from the rating agencies; *Il Sole Ventiquattro Ore* reports that S&P has revised Italy’s outlook from stable to "positive," a move Minister Giorgetti claims proves the country's fiscal credibility. In Sicily, the situation in Niscemi is critical; a three-story building has collapsed into the landslide that is eating the town, with *La Repubblica* confirming the area remains unstable despite the rain finally easing. In the Mediterranean, the government’s clampdown on NGOs continues, with *Libero* noting that the "Sea Watch 5" has been hit with a 20-day administrative detention and a fine after rescuing 18 people. And finally, *Il Messaggero* reports a harsh reality check for road safety: the Ministry of Transport has completed a census of the country's speed cameras, revealing that out of 11,000 devices, only 1,000 are actually homologated, opening the door to a potential tidal wave of appeals. But we must return, for the second day in a row, to the open warfare consuming the Italian judiciary. If yesterday’s inauguration at the Court of Cassation was the opening salvo, today the conflict spread to the district Courts of Appeal across the country, transforming ceremonial speeches into political indictments. The protagonist, once again, was Justice Minister Carlo Nordio. Speaking in Milan, Nordio doubled down on his defense of the separation of careers, using a word that has set the press on fire. He declared it "blasphemous"—his term—to suggest that the government’s reform intends to undermine the independence of the judiciary. The use of religious terminology to describe a constitutional dispute has widened the chasm between the powers of the state. The reaction from the magistrates was synchronized and severe. In Milan, the Prosecutor General called the reform "punitive and useless," arguing it ignores the real issue: a 40% staff shortage. *La Repubblica* frames this as a total rupture, painting Nordio as a minister disconnected from the logistical reality of the courts, intent only on a political vendetta. Conversely, *Il Giornale* and *Libero* are rallying behind the Minister, framing the magistrates’ protests as the last gasp of a politicized caste that refuses to be governed, emphasizing Nordio’s assurance that there is no "persecutory intent." The takeaway here is structural paralysis. While the Minister speaks of "blasphemy" and the magistrates speak of "survival," the actual machinery of justice remains the second slowest in Europe. As *Il Fatto Quotidiano* points out with characteristic cynicism, the "referendum" on this reform is becoming a proxy war for the autonomy of the judicial branch, and today’s synchronized speeches suggest the judiciary is preparing for a total mobilization against the executive. Moving from the war in the courts to the war on the streets. The violence in Turin today was not unexpected, but its political magnitude is significant. What started as a protest against the eviction of the historic "Askatasuna" social center became, as reported by *La Stampa*, a scene of urban warfare. But the crucial detail isn't the burning dumpster or the tear gas; it is the political composition of the march. *Il Giornale* and the right-wing press are heavily emphasizing the presence of parliamentarians from the Green-Left Alliance (AVS) within the corteo, effectively accusing the institutional Left of marching alongside violent anarchists. This creates a sharp narrative split. *Fanpage* and the left-leaning outlets focus on the police tactics and the "militarization" of the city, portraying the march as a defense of spaces for social dissent. The Right, led by *Fratelli d'Italia* voices in *Libero*, is framing this as "Red Terrorism" adjacent, demanding that the Democratic Party and Giuseppe Conte clarify their stance on their coalition partners who march with people throwing firecrackers at police. In Italy, public order is never just about safety; it is always a litmus test for political alliances, and the smoke over Turin is already choking the dialogue in Rome. Meanwhile, turning to the economy, there is a quiet victory being celebrated at the Treasury. While the domestic political scene is chaotic, the international ledger is looking surprisingly clean. *Il Sole Ventiquattro Ore* highlights the S&P decision to upgrade Italy’s outlook to "positive" while confirming the BBB+ rating. This is technically technical, but politically vital. It signals into the markets that Italy's debt, while monstrous, is being managed with enough discipline to reassure foreign investors. *La Verità* adds an interesting layer, noting that Italian exports are holding up better than expected—even to the US—defying fears of a Trump-induced trade squeeze. For the Meloni government, this is ammunition: they can point to the spread and the ratings agencies as proof that the "catastrophe" predicted by the opposition has not arrived. But before we go, we must address a divine controversy in the heart of Rome. In the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Lucina, a newly restored fresco has revealed a cherub that bears a striking, almost photo-realistic resemblance to Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. The discovery has sent the Roman press into a frenzy. As reported by *Corriere della Sera*, the opposition is unamused, with the Democratic Party demanding an inquiry by the Superintendence into whether the restoration was "tampered with" to flatter the leader. The Prime Minister, for her part, chose irony over outrage, posting the photo with the caption: "I definitely do not look like an angel." In a country where politics is a religion, it seems only fitting that the politicians are now literally being painted onto the church ceilings. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-02-01
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-02-01/2026-02-01-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Sunday, February 1st and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. We begin with the blitz. The tragedy in Niscemi deepens as the earth continues to move; *La Repubblica* reports that drones have identified further detachments from the hillside, with the local bishop warning that the town cannot remain inert while citizens lose their homes. In Rome, the tourist experience changes tomorrow morning; *ANSA* confirms that the 2-euro ticket to view the Trevi Fountain goes into effect, a measure the municipality claims is necessary to manage the "overtourism" choking the capital. In the north, the mountains are treacherous; *Il Messaggero* reports a fatal day in the Alps, with avalanches in Friuli claiming the life of a ski-alpinist and burying several others, prompting severe warnings from the Alpine Rescue. On the geopolitical stage, *La Stampa* highlights the tension radiating from Washington to Teheran, noting that the Iranian parliament has designated European armies as "terrorist organizations" in a tit-for-tat retaliation against EU sanctions. And finally, *Il Sole Ventiquattro Ore* offers a rare moment of unity between industry and government, noting that Confindustria is celebrating the S&P ratings outlook upgrade as proof that Italian manufacturing remains resilient despite the German recession. But the main story today is the political fallout from the urban warfare in Turin. If yesterday was about the smoke and the tear gas, today is about the political shrapnel. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni travelled personally to the Molinette Hospital in Turin to visit the police officer who was surrounded and beaten—an image that has dominated the Sunday news cycle. As reported by *Corriere della Sera*, the Premier did not mince words, rejecting the term "demonstration" and reclassifying the event as "attempted murder." This visit has emboldened the Government to launch a full-scale offensive not just against the anarchists, but against the institutional Left. The narrative divide is absolute. *Il Giornale* and *Libero* are ferociously targeting the "Alleanza Verdi e Sinistra" (AVS), specifically Deputy Marco Grimaldi, who was present in the piazza. *Libero* frames the left's presence as a de facto endorsement of "Red Squadrismo," demanding the resignation of local councilors who marched alongside those throwing paper bombs. They are using the graphic video of the officer being beaten with a hammer as proof that the opposition is flirting with 1970s-style terrorism. On the other side, the defense is fractured. While *La Stampa*—the voice of the Turin establishment—acknowledges the "guerrilla" tactics and the fear gripping the city, *Il Manifesto* and *Fanpage* are trying to shift the focus back to the "militarization" of the city and the legitimacy of the social center's existence. However, the optics of the violence have forced the center-left into a defensive crouch, with the Democratic Party struggling to distance itself from the violence without breaking its alliance with the hard left. The takeaway is clear: the government will use the blood on the Turin pavement to fast-track the new Security Decree, framing any opposition to it as complicity with criminals. Moving from political violence to the breakdown of security in the economic capital. Milan is reeling from a violent Sunday in the Rogoredo district, an area infamous for its open-air drug market. As reported by *La Repubblica*, a man disarmed a security guard, beating him with a stick, and then engaged in a shootout with police before being neutralized. While *Il Fatto Quotidiano* focuses on the dynamics of the shooting and the critical condition of the aggressor, the Right is using this to paint a picture of a city out of control. *Il Giornale* employs biting sarcasm, calling the drug dealing and violence the "Olympic Games of Rogoredo," a dark jab at Mayor Beppe Sala’s preparation for the 2026 Winter Games. *La Verità* links this directly to immigration policy, emphasizing the irregularity of the attacker to argue that the state has lost control of its territory. This story matters because it reinforces the "Law and Order" narrative that is currently the government's strongest political asset, putting the milanese administration under immense pressure just as the Olympic spotlight begins to turn toward the city. Meanwhile, a quiet but significant tremor is being felt in the halls of Parliament regarding immigration. While the politicians argue, the public—or at least a very mobilized segment of it—is taking action. *La Verità* triumphantly reports that a petition for a law on "Remigration"—essentially a proposal to enable mass expulsions and incentivize the return of immigrants to their home countries—has gathered over 60,000 signatures in just 24 hours. *Libero* frames this as a direct reaction to the "censorship" attempts by the Left, who tried to block the press conference announcing the initiative. This is a high-consequence signal. *Il Manifesto* views this with alarm, describing it as a "race to the right" that normalizes extremist ideas. The success of this petition serves as a warning shot to the Meloni government from its own right flank: there is a base that feels the current hardened stance on migration is still not hard enough. It creates a new pole of pressure that could force the coalition to adopt even more radical positions to avoid being outflanked by grassroots populism. But before we go, we return to the divine comedy playing out in a Roman basilica. The case of the "Meloni Angel" continues to amuse and annoy the capital. The fresco in the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Lucina, which allegedly bears the face of the Prime Minister, has now triggered a formal request for an inquiry by the Democratic Party, who want to know if the restoration was politically tampered with. *Il Giornale* mocks the "visions" of the Left, quoting the church rector who insists the figures are merely "souls in Purgatory." Whether it is a miraculous apparition or a painter's sycophantic tribute, it serves as a perfect metaphor for modern Italy: a country where politics is so pervasive it literally stares down at you from the ceiling of the church. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-02-03
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-02-03/2026-02-03-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Tuesday 03 and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. We begin with the blitz. Russian missiles have pounded Ukraine’s energy grid in the heaviest attack of the year, just as President Zelensky warns that without power, negotiation tables mean nothing. In Rome, the government’s controversial Security Decree, designed to crack down on street protests, has been delayed until Thursday to iron out constitutional concerns. Tragedy strikes Naples, where a twenty-two-year-old woman, Ilenia Musella, was stabbed to death, allegedly by family members, sparking yet another debate on domestic violence that so far remains strictly local. On the financial front, despite the political noise, the Treasury placed a new fifteen-year BTP bond with record demand exceeding one hundred fifty billion euro, proving the markets are currently ignoring the Palazzo Chigi drama. And finally, the Olympic machine is whirring to life, with President Mattarella in Milan calling for a global truce, while Lindsey Vonn announces she will ski with a broken cruciate ligament—a metaphor, perhaps, for the resilience, or the recklessness, of the entire event. But the story that is actually shaking the foundations of the ruling coalition is the divorce between Matteo Salvini and the General. Roberto Vannacci has officially left the League. The man who wrote "The World Upside Down" and brought half a million preferenze to Salvini’s party in the European elections has decided the vessel is too small for his ego. He has launched his own movement, "Futuro Nazionale," and declared he is walking alone. The spin on this rupture defines the current state of the Italian Right. For the establishment Right and the League’s loyalists, the narrative is one of betrayal and dishonor. *Libero* and *Il Giornale* are running thick with quotes from a "deluded and bitter" Salvini, who reminds the General that "a soldier never abandons his post." *Libero* emphasizes that the League opened its doors when everyone else was cancelling Vannacci, framing his exit as political opportunism devoid of loyalty. *Il Giornale* goes a step further, subtly mocking his new manifesto and warning that the group of "Patriots" in Europe has already expelled him because membership requires a party card, not just a personality cult. However, cross the aisle to *La Repubblica* and *Il Fatto Quotidiano*, and the picture changes from betrayal to implosion. *Repubblica* highlights the schadenfreude of the old Northern League guard, quoting Mario Borghezio who cheers for Vannacci, claiming Salvini has "denatured" the party and deserves the beating. *Il Fatto Quotidiano* asks the only question that matters for the stability of the government: "Who goes with him?" They report that at least three MPs are already considered "Vannacciani" and could follow him out the door. The takeaway here is structural: the League is bleeding support to its right, and if Vannacci siphons off the extremist vote, Salvini’s leverage within the Meloni government—already fragile—could snap entirely. Meanwhile, moving from the corridors of the party headquarters to the streets of Turin, the aftershocks of Saturday’s riots are dictating the legislative agenda in Rome. Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi reported to the Chamber regarding the clashes with the Askatasuna social center. His language was stark. As reported by *Il Giornale* and *La Verità*, Piantedosi described the violence not as a protest, but as a strategy of "urban warfare" reminiscent of the Years of Lead, accusing opposition politicians who attended the march of offering "impunity" to delinquents. The government is using this to fast-track a new Security Decree, which includes a controversial "preventive detention" for those deemed dangerous to public order before crimes are even committed. The opposition, naturally, sees it differently. *La Repubblica* and the Democratic Party accuse the government of using the riots as a pretext for an authoritarian turn, criminalizing dissent rather than addressing the root causes of social anger. But the most interesting detail comes from *La Verità*, which notes the decree was delayed not because of the opposition, but because of doubts from the Quirinale and Forza Italia regarding the constitutionality of banning people from protests without a trial. The government is walking a tightrope between demanding law and order and violating civil liberties. Turning to the economy, while the politicians fight over street battles, the industrial fabric of the country is quietly being redrawn abroad. Deep in the business pages, a story from *Il Corriere della Sera* contrasts sharply with a report from *Il Manifesto*. *Corriere* profiles a Turin-based component manufacturer for the auto industry that is opening a factory in Algeria. The paper frames this as a smart expansion strategy to serve Stellantis, which is growing its footprint in North Africa. It’s presented as Italian ingenuity going global. *Il Manifesto*, however, strips away the gloss, calling it what the unions fear it is: delocalization. While Rome argues about "Made in Italy" and creates commemorative days for pasta, the actual supply chain of the automotive sector—the engine of the north—is drifting across the Mediterranean to chase lower costs, leaving the "Motor City" of Turin increasingly empty. But before we go, a moment of divine comedy from the capital. Visitors to the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Lucina in Rome have noticed something peculiar about a newly restored fresco of an angel. As *L’Unità* and *Corriere della Sera* report with raised eyebrows, the cherub bears an uncanny, photorealistic resemblance to Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. The Vicariate has hurriedly issued a statement saying, quote, "surely the original didn't look like that," while the noblewoman who funded the restoration claims she "doesn't remember." Whether it’s a miracle, a prank by the restorer, or a sycophantic homage, it is the perfect metaphor for a country where politics eventually paints over everything—even the sacred. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-02-04
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-02-04/2026-02-04-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Wednesday 04 and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. We begin with the blitz. In Budapest, the gavel has come down heavy on Maja T., the German activist tried in the same neo-Nazi clash case involving Ilaria Salis; she has been sentenced to eight years in prison, a verdict *La Repubblica* calls a political warning shot from Orbán's Hungary to the European Left. Back in Rome, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has confirmed that Russian hackers have launched cyberattacks targeting both Italian embassies and the digital infrastructure of the Milano-Cortina Olympics, a digital front opening up just days before the torch arrives. Speaking of the Games, it is a bad day for Italy’s soft power: CONI President Giovanni Malagò failed to get elected to the International Olympic Committee’s executive board, defeated in a runoff by a Chilean candidate, a result *Il Fatto Quotidiano* describes as a "burning humiliation" for the Italian establishment. Meanwhile, the controversy over armed US agents on Italian soil for the Olympics seems to be deflating; Minister Piantedosi assured Parliament that the agents will have no operational powers, a statement intended to calm the sovereignist jitter within his own ranks. Finally, tragedy in the Alps, where an avalanche in Tarvisio has claimed a life, a grim reminder from nature amidst the political storms. But the story dominating the front pages is the consummation of the divorce between the Captain and the General. Roberto Vannacci, the vote-magnet of the last European elections, has turned his guns directly on Matteo Salvini. The rupture is total. In his first public appearance since leaving the League, reported gleefully by *La Repubblica* and *La Stampa*, Vannacci reversed the narrative of betrayal. He accuses Salvini of being the *real* traitor to the Right, citing the League’s "prone position" on sending arms to Ukraine and its failure to abolish the Fornero pension law. Vannacci claims his new movement, "Futuro Nazionale," is already polling at over 4 percent—a figure that, if accurate, comes almost entirely out of the League’s hide. The reaction from the pro-government press is a mix of fury and damage control. *Il Giornale* and *Libero* represent the establishment’s shield wall, painting Vannacci as an "ingrate" who used the party as a taxi to Brussels and is now revealing his true, chaotic nature. *Il Giornale* runs quote after quote from League loyalists declaring the "chapter closed," trying to exorcise the General as a mere nuisance. However, the analysis from *Il Messaggero* suggests a deeper panic: if Vannacci’s 4 percent prevents the Center-Right coalition from securing crucial victories in upcoming regional elections, the "ingrate" might just become the kingmaker—or the executioner—of the current majority’s stability. Meanwhile, the shockwaves from the Turin riots are colliding with constitutional hurdles at the Quirinale. Following the violent clashes at the Askatasuna social center, Interior Minister Piantedosi briefed the Senate, rejecting accusations of police provocation and calling the events "urban warfare." While *Il Giornale* headlines with "The Left winks at terrorists," the real political machinery is grinding to a halt behind closed doors. *La Verità* and *Libero* report that the much-vaunted "Security Decree"—which includes harsh preventive detention measures and a crackdown on street blockades—has hit a wall. That wall is President Sergio Mattarella. According to government sources, the Quirinale has expressed serious doubts about the constitutionality of banning citizens from specific areas without a trial and creating "separate jurisprudence" for protesters. *La Repubblica* notes the irony: while Salvini demands "prison for the violent," the judges in Turin actually released two of the arrested protesters and placed only one under house arrest, citing a lack of flight risk. The government is now trapped between its "Law and Order" base and the constitutional guardrails of the Republic, with the Security Decree likely returning to the drawing board for a softening that will infuriate the hardliners. Turning to a quiet revolution that will affect millions of workers, the government is about to break one of the country's oldest taboos: salary secrecy. Buried away from the screaming political headlines, *Il Corriere della Sera* details a new legislative decree landing on the Council of Ministers' table tomorrow. Transposing an EU directive, the new law will give Italian employees the right to request—and receive—written information on the average salary levels of colleagues doing the same work, broken down by gender. It bans "secrecy clauses" in contracts that prevent workers from discussing their pay. For the business establishment, usually represented by *Il Sole 24 Ore*, this is a massive compliance headache requiring new transparency regarding "gender pay gaps." But for the unions and the Left, as echoed in *Fanpage*, this is a potential game-changer in a country where wage stagnation is chronic and pay disparity is often hidden behind a veil of "privacy." In a country where asking "how much do you make?" is considered ruder than asking about someone's sex life, the workplace dynamics are about to get very interesting. But before we go, we return to the Roman church of San Lorenzo in Lucina for the final act of the "Meloni Angel." After days of viral photos showing a newly restored cherub with the unmistakable face of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, the Vatican has stepped in with the eraser. As *L’Unità* reports with evident amusement, the Vicariate ordered the face to be removed, citing "non-conformity with sacred iconography." The restorer, perhaps realizing his prank had gone too far—or not far enough—complied, painting over the Prime Minister’s likeness. It leaves us with a blank space on a fresco, perhaps the only place in Rome right now where Giorgia Meloni’s influence has been successfully curbed. I will see you tomorrow.

item.title: Italy Today - 2026-02-06
item.description: View all sources: https://briefings.my/italy-today/artifacts/2026-02-06/2026-02-06-sources-view.html --- Welcome to another episode of "Italy Today", today is Friday 06 and this episode was curated by Gemini 3 Pro. We begin with the blitz. In Moscow, the shadow war has reached the capital's doorstep; the Vice Chief of Russian Military Intelligence, Major General Vladimir Alekseyev, has been shot and critically wounded in an assassination attempt, a strike that *La Repubblica* calls a "perfect crime" destabilizing the Kremlin's security apparatus. Closer to home, the industrial pride of Italy has taken a severe beating; Stellantis stock has crashed by nearly 25% in Milan, wiping out billions in value after announcing a dividend suspension and massive costs linked to the electric transition. In the halls of Parliament, the League is bleeding from the right flank; two MPs have defected to join General Roberto Vannacci’s new political movement, "Futuro Nazionale," signaling the start of a dangerous fragmentation within the government coalition. Across the Atlantic, a cultural firestorm has erupted after Donald Trump posted—and then deleted—a racist AI video depicting the Obamas, a move *La Stampa* describes as "institutional delirium." Finally, the "Justice War" escalates, as the Court of Cassation has officially greenlit the new referendum question on separating careers in the judiciary, backed by 500,000 signatures, setting the stage for a spring showdown at the ballot box. But the eyes of the world are fixed on Milan tonight, where the Winter Olympics are set to begin not just with a torch, but with a masterclass in populism and high-wire diplomacy. The opening ceremony at San Siro is the main event, but the real show started hours earlier on the city’s rails. In a move calculated to puncture the narrative of elitism often surrounding the games, President Sergio Mattarella arrived at the stadium not in a motorcade, but aboard a historic Milanese tram, driven by none other than MotoGP legend Valentino Rossi. *Corriere della Sera* frames this as a brilliant stroke of "institutional normalcy," a symbolic hug to a city under siege by construction sites and traffic. However, the unity in the tram contrasts sharply with the tension in the VIP box. While Mattarella plays the benevolent grandfather of the nation, Prime Minister Giornato Meloni is navigating a diplomatic minefield with U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance. The narrative surrounding these games is fracturing along predictable political lines. While *Il Giornale* and *Libero* are busy celebrating the "Italian Miracle" and the organizational resilience of Milan-Cortina, the opposition press is looking at the cracks in the ice. *Il Fatto Quotidiano* is highlighting the protests at the PalaSharp, where antagonists have occupied the space to denounce the "cementification of the mountains" and the militarization of the city. Furthermore, a cultural skirmish is brewing over the artist Ghali, who will perform tonight. After weeks of polemics regarding his pro-Palestinian stance, *La Repubblica* reports he will recite a poem by Gianni Rodari against war, a choice that Minister Valditara, quoted in *Libero*, dismissed by saying he "doesn't want to talk about controversies on a day of celebration," effectively trying to silence the noise before the anthem plays. Moving from the fanfare of the stadium to the panic on the trading floor, the industrial pillar of the country is shaking. Stellantis has suffered what financial analysts are calling a "bloodbath." The stock plummeted nearly 25% after the automotive giant warned it burnt through 22 billion euros trying to manage a slowing electric vehicle market and would suspend dividends. *Il Sole 24 Ore* delivers the cold, hard math: the transition to electric is costing more than expected, and the market is punishing the uncertainty. But the political fallout is where the story gets interesting. *La Stampa*, historically the voice of the Turin industrial establishment, treats this as a tragedy for Italian labor, amplifying CEO Antonio Filosa's admission of "too many errors." However, the spin from the Right is aggressive and distinct. *La Verità* leads with a cynical take on Chairman John Elkann, noting that after years of "green rhetoric," the company is now writing to Brussels to demand protectionism and subsidies to survive the Asian competition. The paper accuses the Agnelli-Elkann dynasty of socializing losses while privatizing profits, framing the crash not just as a business failure, but as the collapse of the "Green Deal" ideology itself. The government is watching closely; if Stellantis sneezes, the Italian supply chain catches pneumonia. Turning our attention to the courts, a dormant volcano has just woken up. The Supreme Court of Cassation has accepted the signatures for the referendum on the "Separation of Careers" for magistrates, a reform that would structurally divide judges from prosecutors. This is the "Mother of all Reforms" for the Justice Ministry. *Il Giornale* is cheering this as the beginning of the end for the "politicized judiciary," arguing that the people will finally break the caste system within the courts. Minister Nordio, feeling the wind in his sails, is quoted telling the press that victory is certain. Conversely, *Il Fatto Quotidiano* and *La Repubblica* are sounding the alarm, framing this as a government plot to subjugate the judiciary under the guise of efficiency. With the referendum potentially slated for spring, the country is bracing for a polarizing campaign that will pit the government directly against the robes of the state. But before we go, we must address a diplomatic incident that is equal parts embarrassing and hilarious. While Vice President Vance was in Milan meeting Prime Minister Meloni, the U.S. State Department released an official readout of the lunch that contained a glaring error. As reported with some glee by *La Stampa*, the American document listed the participants as "The Vice President and Mrs. Meloni," and then, inexplicably, listed a "Mr. Meloni" as her spouse. The problem? Giorgia Meloni is not married, and she certainly didn't bring a phantom husband to a diplomatic summit. The "spouse" listed was actually a misidentified member of the entourage. It was a clerical error that forced a hasty correction from Washington, proving that while American intelligence might know about Russian generals, their knowledge of the Italian Premier's relationship status leaves something to be desired. I will see you tomorrow.
